title: Toaster, toaster oven or air fryer: safe teardown
summary: Take the heating elements, thermostat, timer and switches, convection fan, door glass, racks and trays out of a toaster, toaster oven or air fryer. The dangers are mains wiring, sharp sheet-metal edges, and toughened door glass that can shatter without warning.

steps.text: Unplug it, keep the plug where you can see it, and let it cool until the back of your hand, held near the elements and case, feels no heat. Slide out the crumb tray, racks and trays and set them aside: they are the easiest salvage.
steps.warn: Never reach into a toaster's slots or an oven cavity while it is plugged in. The bare elements are live at mains voltage.

steps.text: Pull the knobs straight off. If one sticks, lever it with two flat blades, one on each side.

Turn it over on a towel and undo the screws in the base and back. Some hide under rubber feet: pry the feet out. Some ovens and air fryers use Torx or security Torx with a centre pin. Pop-up toasters are often held by bent metal tabs: straighten them with pliers.
steps.warn: Sheet-metal edges are sharp. Wear gloves.

steps.text: Lift the outer cover off. On a toaster oven the cover comes off differently on each model: look for tabs, and for a screw on the door frame, before you pull. On a pop-up toaster the top may stay hooked to a spring: hold the top, unhook the spring with pliers and keep your face clear, because it can flick back.

Digital ovens, air fryers and pop-up toasters with an electronic timer have a circuit board. Wait at least 5 minutes after unplugging. Discharge every capacitor on it that is rated over 50 V, or has no readable rating, with a resistor tool (see safety_discharge_capacitor), then measure DC volts across it to prove it is empty. Then photograph all the wiring.
steps.warn: Unplugged does not mean discharged. Discharge first, then prove with the meter that the capacitor is empty before you touch the board.

steps.text: Look at the insulation before you touch the elements. In a very old toaster or oven, grey or white fibrous board, pads or wrapping on the elements or wires may be asbestos. If you see any, stop: don't break it, scrape it or blow dust off it, and read safety_asbestos_check. Pick a newer unit.

Take the timer and selector switch from behind their knobs. Press the metal tab on each push-on connector with pliers and pull it off, then undo the two small screws holding each control to the front panel.
Take the thermostat behind the temperature knob the same way. Label its wires as they come off.
Toaster oven elements: pull the connectors off both ends, unfold the metal tabs holding the element, and slide it out through the cavity wall. Hold quartz tubes by their metal ends only.
steps.warn: Quartz tubes are glass: they shatter if knocked, flexed or dropped. Wear eye protection and gloves. Pick up broken pieces with tape or a damp cloth, never bare fingers.

steps.text: Pop-up toaster elements: the element wire is on mica plates fixed to the frame. Unhook or cut the wires at the back and lift each plate out whole. Bend back or drill out the rivets only if you must.
steps.warn: Mica plates are brittle. Flex them as little as you can.

steps.text: Pop-up toasters: take the control board with the electromagnet beside the lever, the lever switch and the springs. Let the lever up first so the carriage spring is relaxed, hold each spring as you unhook it, and keep your face clear.

Fans: in an air fryer, take off the motor bracket first (two long screws and a silver piece) and set the motor aside, then loosen the bolt behind the heating plate, remove the screw holding it, and work the fan out from under it. A second fan may sit under a metal dome. In a convection oven the fan is behind a cover at the back or side of the cavity.
steps.warn: Air fryer fan blades have sharp edges.

steps.text: Door glass: undo the hinge or frame screws, or bend open the frame tabs, and slide the glass out. Wrap it in cloth and carry it on edge.
steps.warn: Toughened glass can burst into small pieces, even long after a knock. Wear gloves and eye protection. Never cut, drill or clamp it, and keep it where it can't fall on anyone.

steps.text: Test each part you kept with the meter (see the notes), and label it OK or BAD.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Heating elements.** Three kinds turn up. Pop-up toasters use nichrome wire on mica plates (iFixit toaster problems). Toaster ovens use quartz glass tubes in the Breville BOV800XL (Breville BOV800XL manual). Other models may use metal-sheathed rods: check yours. Each is built for mains voltage. Use it at the voltage on its label, from a generator or a big inverter: a dump load for spare solar, a dehydrator or a small oven. On 12 V they are almost useless: watts = volts × volts ÷ ohms, so a 35 Ω toaster element (iFixit Oster TSSTJC5BBK) gives about 4 W at 12 V.
- **Thermostat.** The heat control behind the temperature knob switches the elements on and off. Keep it with an element to hold a box at a set heat. Check the dial markings for its range.
- **Timer and selector switches.** Basic ovens have a timer and selector held to the front panel by two small screws each (iFixit Bella timer, iFixit Black+Decker TO1303SB). They switch mains current, so they suit heaters and lamps. Digital ovens use an LCD and electronic dials instead of a timer knob (Breville BOV800XL manual), with a circuit board behind them (iFixit BOV800XL relay board).
- **Convection fan and motor.** A small mains motor with a blade. It suits a food dryer or a small vent. Read the label for voltage and watts.
- **Door glass.** The maker says the glass is treated for strength but is not unbreakable: a hard knock can weaken it, and it may later break into many small pieces with no obvious cause (Breville BOV800XL manual). It makes a good window for a solar oven or cold frame (see build_solar_oven). You can't cut it to size; build the frame around it.
- **Racks and trays.** Plain wire racks make grill grates over a fire. Keep non-stick and enamel pans for oven use, away from open flames.
- **Electromagnet (pop-up toasters).** A small coil on the control board holds the lever down until the timer releases it (iFixit Finelife toaster). Keep it with its board if you want a small latch.

## Variations

- **Pop-up toasters.** The Finelife NV-023172 has an electronic timer board with a rectifier, a stop button, a potentiometer and the electromagnet; its elements are riveted to insulating boards on the frame (iFixit Finelife toaster). The Oster TSSTJC5BBK has three elements wired in parallel, each given as 35 Ω in the teardown, on 120 V. Its lever switch is held down mechanically, and its case comes apart by tabs and a spring (iFixit Oster TSSTJC5BBK). On some toasters the electronics get their power through the element circuit, so a broken element stops the lever staying down (iFixit toaster problems).
- **Basic toaster ovens.** The Bella 4-slice has two elements held by bendable metal tabs, and its cover comes off after five rear screws, one on the door frame and four under the feet (iFixit Bella element). The Black+Decker TO1303SB uses T15 Torx screws; the TO1313SB needs security T15 bits with a centre pin. The guide says a failed timer means buying a new oven (iFixit Black+Decker TO1303SB).
- **Smart ovens.** The Breville BOV800XL has five quartz elements and a convection fan, and the maker's page quotes 1,800 W for preheating (Breville BOV800 page, Breville BOV800XL manual). Its relay board holds small transistors and a triac. In one unit hit by lightning, a transistor, a diode and a varistor were the parts that failed (iFixit BOV800XL relay board).
- **Air fryers.** The Ninja AF161 is 1,750 W at 120 V (iFixit Ninja AF161). Its heating plate sits over one fan, with a second fan under a metal dome. Six of its screws need a TR15 Torx bit (iFixit Ninja AF161 fan).

## Testing what you got out

Do every test on a part that is out of the oven, or with one wire taken off (see test_continuity).

- **Elements.** Set the meter to ohms. Expected ohms are about volts × volts ÷ watts. A 220 V, 600 W toaster reads about 80 Ω and a 1,200 W one about 40 Ω (iFixit toaster problems). OL means the wire is broken: follow it along the mica to find the break. Then test from each end to the metal frame or sheath: anything but OL means a short, so scrap it. A cold reading may not match the formula, which uses the rated figure. Judge quartz tubes and other elements by open or shorted, not by the exact number.
- **Thermostat and switches.** Turn the knob through its range. The reading should flip cleanly between about 0 Ω and OL.
- **Thermal fuses**, if you find one: a small metal or ceramic cylinder on two leads, with a rated temperature on the body (SEFUSE ones also show a rated current). Test it with the meter only, and never heat it to see if it opens. Good reads close to 0 Ω; OL means it has blown. It is one-shot and can't be reset. A good reading does not prove it will still open at the right temperature, because heat close to its rating wears it out for good (SCHOTT SEFUSE). Don't rely on a salvaged one as the only protection on anything you build, and never bridge a blown one with wire.
- **Electromagnet.** Read its coil in ohms. OL means the coil is broken (iFixit toaster problems).
- **Fan motor.** Spin it by hand: it should turn freely. Its winding should read a steady number of ohms, not OL.

## What to leave

- Cracked quartz tubes and chipped door glass.
- Grey or white fibrous board, pads or wrapping in a very old toaster or oven. EPA lists toasters and ovens among older appliances that used asbestos (EPA asbestos legacy uses). Don't break it or brush dust off it; see safety_asbestos_check.
- Torn heat shielding and the thin painted case, unless you need sheet metal.
- Control boards, unless you want the relays and triac for a build.
